opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that you start with a hypothesis about the structure of the concept itself, before you ever look at the model. Take something like days of the week or months of the year. There's a natural geometry there: it's cyclical, Monday is next to Tuesday, December wraps back around to January. So if the model represents that concept in a way that reflects its real structure, you'd expect a circle or some low-dimensional curved shape in activation space, not just seven or twelve unrelated directions.

The supervised part is that you build a dataset where you know the label for every example. You generate lots of prompts where the relevant token is a specific month or a specific day, in varied contexts, and you collect the activations at some layer. Then, instead of running unsupervised dimensionality reduction and hoping the structure falls out, you fit a mapping from the activations to the coordinates you hypothesized. You're asking directly whether there's a subspace where these points sit on a circle in the right order. Sometimes that's a linear probe onto a low-dimensional target. Sometimes you fit a smooth curve or spline through the class means and look at how tightly the individual examples cluster around it.

Finding a shape you were looking for isn't very convincing on its own, though. With enough dimensions and a flexible enough probe, you can find almost anything. So validation is really the heart of it, and I think about it on a few levels.

First, held-out generalization. Does the manifold you fit on one set of prompts hold up on prompts with different templates and contexts? If it only works on your training distribution, you've probably found something about your dataset, not about the model.

Second, controls. Shuffle the labels and refit. If you still get a nice clean circle, your method is too powerful and the result means nothing. You also want to compare against random subspaces of the same dimensionality.

Third, and most important to me, causal intervention. If the model is actually using this manifold, then moving an activation along it should change the model's behavior in a predictable way. Take a representation of "March," push it along the curve toward where "May" sits, and see whether downstream computations, like "what month comes two after this," shift accordingly. Moving along the manifold should give you smooth, sensible changes, and moving off it should either do nothing or break things. That on-manifold versus off-manifold contrast is strong evidence that the geometry is real and functional, not something your analysis imposed.

The broader point is that a lot of interpretability work has assumed concepts are directions, points along a single line. I think the manifold view is richer and closer to how these models actually organize information, especially for concepts with continuous or relational structure. The supervised approach lets you test that rigorously, as long as you're disciplined about ruling out the cases where you're just seeing your own assumptions reflected back.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it, the starting point is always a hypothesis. You have some concept in mind, say, the model's representation of a person's gender, or sentiment, or whether a statement is true, and you're asking: is there a structured subspace in the residual stream where that concept lives, and does it have geometry that actually means something?

The supervised approach is the most direct way to get at that. You build a dataset where you control the concept and vary everything else. So for something like sentiment, you'd want thousands of inputs that span positive to negative, but with lots of diversity in topic, length, style, so that the only consistent thing the labels track is the concept you care about. That's the part people underestimate. If your positive examples are all about puppies and your negative examples are all about taxes, you're going to find a puppies-versus-taxes direction and call it sentiment.

Then you collect activations at some layer, usually the residual stream at the final token or mean-pooled over tokens, and you fit something simple. A linear probe is the default. If a logistic regression on the activations separates your labels well, that tells you the concept is at least linearly decodable at that layer. But decodable isn't the same as used. That's the key distinction for me. A probe can pick up on information that's present but inert, stuff the model has encoded but never acts on.

So validation has to be causal. The move is to take the direction the probe found and intervene on it. You add or subtract along that direction, or you project it out entirely, and you see whether the model's behavior shifts in the way the concept predicts. If I push along what I'm calling the sentiment direction and the model's outputs get more positive in a controlled, dose-dependent way, that's real evidence. If I ablate it and the model can no longer distinguish positive from negative in downstream tasks, even stronger.

The manifold part comes in when you stop assuming it's a single direction. A lot of concepts aren't binary. Something like a person's age, or a date, or a position on a number line, you'd expect those to be represented with some continuous structure, and in some cases we've seen things that look circular or helical rather than linear. So for those, the supervised setup is the same, but instead of fitting a classifier you're fitting a regression or looking at how activations for ordered labels are laid out in a low-dimensional projection. You check whether the geometry respects the ordering. Does moving from age twenty to age forty in the data correspond to moving smoothly along a curve in activation space? And again, you validate by intervening at points along that curve and seeing if the model's behavior tracks it.

The failure modes I worry about most are the confounds I mentioned, and overfitting. With high-dimensional activations and a modest dataset, a probe can achieve great accuracy by memorizing noise. So I always want to hold out data, test on distribution shifts, and ideally confirm that the same direction generalizes across layers or across prompt formats the probe never saw. If a direction only works on the exact template you trained it on, you've found an artifact, not a concept.

And then there's an honest limitation, which is that the supervised approach can only find what you already thought to look for. It's great for confirming hypotheses and terrible for discovering the concepts the model actually uses that you didn't anticipate. That's where the unsupervised methods come in, but I think the two are complementary. You use unsupervised tools to generate candidates, and then you bring back the supervised machinery to pin down and causally validate the ones that matter.

astra-6.text:
I’d think of it as two separate problems: can we find a representation that predicts the concept, and does that representation actually play a role in how the model uses the concept?

For the supervised part, you start with examples where the concept is present and examples where it isn’t, collect activations, and train a probe to distinguish them. A linear probe is a useful starting point, but it’s making a fairly strong assumption about the geometry. The concept might be represented across multiple directions, or in a way that depends on context.

The challenge is that your probe can learn a shortcut. If all your positive examples share a particular word or writing style, you might be detecting that rather than the concept you care about. So you want varied examples, carefully matched negatives, and held-out tests that change the topic or phrasing while preserving the concept.

Then I’d want to intervene. If you modify the activations along the representation you’ve identified, does the model’s behavior change in the way you’d predict? And can you do that without broadly disrupting unrelated behavior? That’s stronger evidence than probe accuracy alone.

Even then, I’d be cautious about calling it *the* concept manifold. You’ve found a candidate representation with some predictive and causal evidence behind it. Establishing its geometry, and how consistently it works across contexts, is another layer of validation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the supervised approach is to start with a concept that you can label, and then ask whether there’s some structure in the model’s activations that reliably corresponds to it. You collect examples where the concept is present and examples where it isn’t, run those through the model, and train a probe to distinguish them.

But finding a probe that works is really just the beginning. You want to know whether it’s picking up the concept or some correlated feature of your dataset. So you test it on different wording, different contexts, and examples designed to break those correlations. If you’re studying honesty, for example, you don’t want a detector that’s actually just recognizing the topic of the question.

Then there’s a separate question: is this structure something the model actually uses? That’s where interventions become useful. If you change the activations along the structure you’ve identified, does the model’s behavior change in the way you’d predict? And does that change stay specific to the concept?

I’d also be careful about assuming that the concept is a single direction. A linear probe is a useful starting point, but the representation could depend on context or have more complicated geometry. So I’d treat the manifold as a hypothesis, and validate it through both generalization and causal interventions.
